title: A Faster Website Page Speed Starts With a Lighter First View
summary: Improve website page speed by reducing oversized assets, testing mobile loading, reviewing browser caching, and removing unnecessary third-party scripts.
body_markdown:
A page can look complete in the editor yet feel unfinished to a visitor waiting on a phone. The delay may come from one oversized hero, several hidden slides, a video, a font, or an external widget. Website page speed improves when the team identifies which work blocks useful content instead of chasing one score without context.


Reducing oversized website assets lowers the amount a browser must transfer. Improving mobile loading performance checks whether essential content survives a smaller screen and weaker connection. Optimizing browser caching settings helps repeat visits avoid unnecessary downloads, while reducing unnecessary third-party scripts limits work controlled by outside services.


## Read a slow page in four checkpoints


1. **Display:**


How soon can a visitor see the main heading, essential image, and primary action?


2. **Transfer:**


Which images, videos, fonts, or files account for most downloaded bytes?


3. **Execute:**


Which scripts keep the browser busy or delay interaction?


4. **Repeat:**


Which unchanged resources are downloaded again on a return visit?


This sequence turns website page speed into a diagnosis. Reducing oversized website assets addresses transfer weight. Improving mobile loading performance tests display under realistic constraints. Reducing unnecessary third-party scripts reduces execution work, and optimizing browser caching settings concerns what a returning browser can reuse.


## Establish a baseline before changing the page


*Strikingly's Google Pagespeed*


Test the published URL, not only the editor preview. Record the device profile, connection, location, browser, test time, and page version. Run several measurements because network and server conditions vary. Website page speed should be compared against a consistent baseline, not a single good or bad result.


For website page speed, start with the business-critical route: homepage to service, campaign to form, category to product, or product to checkout. When improving mobile loading performance, note when main content appears, input works, and layout shifts. The metric is how soon a visitor can continue.


The Strikingly guide to


[improving site page load speed](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/206051562-Improving-Your-Site-Page-Load-Speed)


recommends lightweight pages, fewer media elements, restrained sliders, careful fonts, and reducing unnecessary third-party scripts. Its article on


[diagnosing website loading speed](https://www.strikingly.com/blog/posts/common-issues-causing-website-loading-speed-diagnose-fix-performance)


connects image weight, requests, delivery, monitoring, and optimizing browser caching settings.


Test once in a normal browser and once in a private window. The difference helps separate first-visit transfer from repeat-visit reuse. This is useful when optimizing browser caching settings, but clearing a cache is a troubleshooting step, not a lasting speed improvement. A new visitor still needs an efficient first load.


## Cut transfer weight where visitors feel it first


*CosmoBrew Template from Strikingly*


Reducing oversized website assets should begin above the fold. List every hero image, background, logo, icon, font, animation, and video requested before the first useful action appears. Remove decorative files that do not help orientation, trust, or the decision. A smaller first view often creates a larger improvement than compressing dozens of assets far below it.


For website page speed, reducing oversized website assets starts by resizing images near their displayed dimensions. Use JPEG for photographs and PNG when transparency is necessary; animated GIFs can be disproportionately heavy. Strikingly reduces uploaded image sizes, but many images can still slow mobile pages. The


[Strikingly Image Editor](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/21524558894619-Strikingly-s-Image-Editor)


supports resizing and cropping, while the


[background image guidelines](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/214364898-Background-Sizes-Settings-Guidelines-for-background-images)


cover dimensions and display settings.


Reducing oversized website assets also means questioning quantity. A carousel may request several large slides even when most visitors never see the later ones. A gallery preview can link to a focused portfolio page. One video can be presented with a text or image link to a larger library. Preserve access to useful media without making every visitor download everything immediately.


### Give the first view a resource budget


Define what must appear immediately, what can wait until interaction or scrolling, and what belongs on another page. Review any new media against that budget. Reducing oversized website assets becomes an editorial decision made before upload instead of an emergency cleanup after a speed report.


## Test the mobile path as a separate performance case


*Strikingly Landing Page on Mobile*


Improving mobile loading performance requires more than narrowing a desktop browser. Test a real phone when possible, use a slower network profile, and begin with an empty cache. Watch whether the heading appears before large media, whether consent tools cover the screen, whether late content shifts the button, and whether the page remains responsive while scripts initialize.


Prioritize the content a mobile visitor needs to decide or continue. Move heavy galleries, maps, social feeds, and videos below the primary explanation when they are not essential. Improving mobile loading performance often comes from changing sequence and quantity, not merely shrinking everything to fit.


Website page speed on responsive templates still depends on improving mobile loading performance and reducing oversized website assets. The


[pre-publish checklist](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/214364618-Pre-publish-Checklist)


recommends mobile previews plus checks for backgrounds, links, section order, and unused content. The guide for a


[site that looks strange on mobile](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/215046907-Website-looks-strange-on-mobile)


identifies masked forwarding and background settings as possible causes.


Improving mobile loading performance should be checked on the pages reached from advertisements, email, search, and social profiles. Those entry pages may carry campaign pixels, embeds, or large creative assets that the homepage does not. Compare first content, first interaction, and completion behavior for each important route.


## Treat caching as a delivery policy, not a magic switch


For website page speed, optimizing browser caching settings means reusing stable resources for an appropriate period while allowing changed files to refresh. Logos, fonts, scripts, and styles may benefit repeat visits; frequently changing data may need shorter reuse. Policy depends on ownership and versioning.


On a hosted builder, the platform manages core delivery, compression, and much of the caching behavior. Do not paste generic server configuration into a page and expect it to change response headers. For a Strikingly site, optimizing browser caching settings is mainly an audit of custom-hosted files, external widgets, and vendor resources, while relying on the platform for its own assets.


Use the browser network panel to inspect repeat requests. Reload once with an empty cache, then reload normally and compare transferred bytes. If an unchanged custom resource downloads in full each time, ask its host or developer whether cache headers and versioned filenames are appropriate. Optimizing browser caching settings should never serve obsolete content indefinitely.


Separate caching problems from publishing problems. A stale local view may be tested in private mode or another supported browser, as Strikingly's


[supported browser guide](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/206256982-Strikingly-Supported-Browsers)


suggests. Optimizing browser caching settings may identify stale local data; it does not replace reducing oversized website assets.


## Put every third-party script on trial


*Strikingly App Store HTML Integration*


Reducing unnecessary third-party scripts begins with an inventory. List analytics tags, chat tools, pixels, maps, video players, consent managers, and custom embeds. Record the owner, page coverage, business purpose, last use, and removal risk. Reducing unnecessary third-party scripts also means removing unknown code that remains only because the page still loads.


### Ask four questions when reducing unnecessary third-party scripts


1. Does it support a current customer or measurement need?


2. Must it load on every page, or only where the feature appears?


3. Can a link, static preview, or delayed interaction replace the immediate embed?


4. Who will review the vendor, consent requirement, and performance cost again?


Strikingly's


[custom code guide](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/215046517-Add-Custom-Code-HTML-CSS-and-JavaScript)


explains header, footer, and HTML-section locations, while the


[HTML Embed guide](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/215046527)


covers page-level applications. Reducing unnecessary third-party scripts includes checking all of these locations and documenting why each integration remains.


Measure before removal, remove one integration, publish, and test the same route again. Confirm that forms, attribution, consent, and customer support still work. Improving mobile loading performance often benefits because slower devices spend less time parsing and executing outside code. Reducing unnecessary third-party scripts should protect essential functions, not create silent operational failur


## Keep the page simple enough to remain fast


Website page speed is easier to protect when each page has one job. Split unrelated topics instead of extending a homepage indefinitely. Reducing unnecessary third-party scripts, sliders, background videos, custom fonts, and decorative effects lowers requests while giving visitors a clearer choice.


Reducing oversized website assets should become part of publishing review. Improving mobile loading performance belongs in campaign quality assurance. Optimizing browser caching settings belongs in technical review for custom resources, and reducing unnecessary third-party scripts requires an owner and renewal date. These responsibilities prevent speed work from becoming an occasional cleanup.


## Measure the route again after publishing


Retest the same URLs, devices, and network profiles after each meaningful change. Record what was removed, resized, moved, or delayed. Website page speed improves through controlled comparisons; changing images, layout, scripts, and copy simultaneously makes the result difficult to explain.


Use


[Strikingly built-in analytics](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/215752348-Using-Your-Strikingly-Built-in-Analytics)


and


[Google Analytics 4 with Strikingly](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/15275247898395-Using-Google-Analytics-with-Strikingly-GA4)


to watch engagement and conversions after changes. Pair behavior with technical tests for improving mobile loading performance and optimizing browser caching settings. A score matters when visitors reach useful content and complete the intended action reliably.


Schedule a review after campaigns, redesigns, app installations, and large content updates. Reducing oversized website assets may catch a new uncompressed hero. Reducing unnecessary third-party scripts may identify an expired campaign pixel. Optimizing browser caching settings may reveal a custom asset host that changed its policy, while improving mobile loading performance may expose a new overlay or embed that blocks the first action.


Choose one high-value mobile entry page today. Capture its baseline, remove the largest unnecessary cost, publish, and repeat the same test. That narrow cycle makes website page speed understandable, measurable, and easier to preserve as the site grows.
